content: Home visits by community health workers (CHWs) during the first week of life, when combined with other interventions such as prenatal visits and community mobilization activities, have been shown to significantly reduce neonatal and perinatal mortality rates. These findings are based on studies conducted in South Asia, with additional data from African settings still pending. No evidence of harm associated with home visits has been reported. Health providers, policymakers, and families in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) highly value these interventions, especially in settings where early hospital discharge (within 24 hours of birth) is common, followed by home visits for postnatal care. However, implementing such programs requires careful planning and resource allocation, particularly in LMICs where health professional shortages may necessitate the use of CHWs instead of midwives. Danger signs in newborns, such as fever, jaundice, or difficulty breathing, should prompt families to seek immediate healthcare. Algorithms based on simple clinical signs, used by CHWs during postnatal visits, have been evaluated in community-based studies in India. These algorithms demonstrated varying levels of sensitivity and specificity in identifying severe illnesses requiring referral. Among the tested algorithms, the YIS-2 algorithm showed the best balance of sensitivity and specificity for detecting severe illness during postnatal care. Modifications to this algorithm, as suggested by study authors, may further improve its performance. Exclusive breastfeeding (EBF) is strongly recommended for all infants from birth until six months of age. Evidence indicates that EBF reduces the risk of neonatal mortality and morbidity, including infections such as sepsis, respiratory infections, and diarrhea, compared to partial breastfeeding. Mothers should receive counseling and support for EBF during all antenatal and postnatal contacts, particularly in cases of preterm or low-birth-weight infants or after cesarean delivery. EBF is a low-cost intervention with significant health benefits. For newborns born at home in high neonatal mortality settings, the application of chlorhexidine to the umbilical cord stump during the first week of life is recommended to reduce neonatal mortality and omphalitis. Clean, dry cord care is advised for facility births and low-mortality settings. Chlorhexidine use may also replace harmful traditional substances applied to the cord stump. However, its use may delay cord separation time, and its application should not interfere with essential newborn care practices such as skin-to-skin contact and early breastfeeding initiation. Bathing of newborns should be delayed for at least 24 hours after birth, or at least six hours if cultural practices prevent further delay. Newborns should be dressed appropriately for the ambient temperature, with one to two layers more than adults, and hats or caps should be used. Rooming-in of the mother and baby 24 hours a day is recommended, along with encouraging communication and play with the newborn. Postnatal care for mothers should include regular assessments of vaginal bleeding, uterine contraction, fundal height, temperature, and heart rate during the first 24 hours after birth. Subsequent postnatal visits should assess urinary and bowel function, perineal wound healing, breastfeeding progress, and emotional well-being. Women should be encouraged to report any changes in mood or behavior and to seek help for symptoms of postpartum depression if they persist beyond 10–14 days after birth. Women should also be counseled on nutrition, hygiene (especially handwashing), family planning, and safer sex practices. In malaria-endemic areas, mothers and babies should sleep under insecticide-treated bed nets. Early mobilization and gentle exercise are encouraged during the postnatal period. Iron and folic acid supplementation should be provided for at least three months after delivery to prevent postpartum anemia, a common issue in high maternal mortality settings. While some women may experience mild side effects from oral iron supplements, the benefits of reducing anemia outweigh these risks. Policymakers value the prevention and treatment of anemia, particularly in countries with widespread nutritional deficiencies. The use of prophylactic antibiotics is recommended for women with thirdor fourth-degree perineal tears following vaginal delivery to prevent wound complications. However, there is insufficient evidence to recommend routine antibiotic use for all low-risk women after vaginal delivery to prevent endometritis.
